one_liner: C++20 compile-time perfect-hash lookup built on BMI2 pext; 2.4-10x lower latency than std::unordered_map on 5-100-key string sets.
what_it_does: Maps a set of keys fixed at compile time to values with no collisions. Keys can be integers, enums, or strings up to 16 bytes, passed as a constexpr std::array of keys or key/value pairs. It is not a container. The API is two function objects: mph::lookup<entries>(key) returns the value and assumes the key is in the set, and mph::find<entries>(key[, unknown]) checks the key and returns an optional-like result. A plain array of keys maps each key to its index 0..N-1, and both calls work in constant expressions.
how_it_is_fast: All table construction happens at compile time. For very small sets, lookup uses a PCG generator to search for a multiplier such that (key*magic)>>shift picks a bit-field out of one 32/64-bit constant, so the lookup is a multiply, a shift and a mask with no memory access. Otherwise it greedily finds the smallest bit mask that keeps every key unique; at run time, BMI2 PEXT packs those bits into a dense index into a 2^popcount(mask) table, and find does one full-key compare (a cmov by default). Strings up to 16 bytes are loaded as one integer (memcpy plus BZHI to trim the length), so there is no per-character hashing or probe loop, and find on more than 64 entries does a single std::experimental::simd bucket compare.
when_to_use: Hot-path mapping of a fixed set of short keys known at build time: keyword or command parsing, string_to_enum/enum_to_string, ticker-symbol or message-type dispatch (the README examples).
Sets of a few keys up to about a thousand. The README latency tables cover 5-100 string keys; the author's plot-only benchmark goes to 1024 keys.
Strings of 8 bytes or fewer, and ideally 4 or fewer (the FAQ says a smaller maximum length gives a smaller table and one fewer instruction), or integer keys as u32/u64.
x86-64 with fast PEXT (Intel Haswell+ or AMD Zen3+ per the FAQ), built with -mbmi2 or -march=native.
Inputs that are always in the set: mph::lookup (or find<100>) skips the key compare and, for tiny integer sets, compiles to 3-5 instructions (README asm).
when_not_to_use: Keys that are only known, or change, at run time. There is no insert, erase or iteration; the table is generated at compile time.

Long keys. Keys must fit in 128 bits (16 bytes), or lookup/find are removed by SFINAE and you must write your own fallback policy (issues #5 and #6 are still open). The mask search also looks at only the low 64 bits (mask<u64>), so keys that share their first 8 bytes can fail (issue #3).
MSVC or libc++. The requirements list only GCC 12+ and Clang 15+, and the header uses GCC/Clang builtins. Open PR #19 reports that main does not compile with libc++'s partial <experimental/simd>.
Large sets. The FAQ says it handles thousands of keys, not millions; build time grows with size and can hit constexpr step limits.
CPUs with slow PEXT (AMD Zen2 takes 18 cycles per the FAQ) or non-x86 targets. Both use the software pext fallback, and no run-time numbers are published for it.

integration.dependencies: none (optional <experimental/simd> from libstdc++, which find needs for sets of more than 64 entries)
integration.min_toolchain: C++20; GCC 12+ or Clang 15+ (README). A C++20 module wrapper, mph.cppm, is also provided.
integration.platforms: x86-64 is the target (BMI2 optional but recommended; AVX2/AVX-512 used through std::experimental::simd); other targets, including arm-none-eabi since issue #14, use a software pext fallback; GCC/Clang only
integration.thread_safety: not documented; lookup and find are noexcept and read only immutable constexpr tables

gotchas: mph::lookup returns an arbitrary value for a key that is not in the set. Use mph::find for untrusted input. find<100> (probability = 100) also skips the compare, so it behaves the same way.

The header runs its self-tests as static_asserts every time you include it; define -DNTEST to skip them. Large sets can hit 'constexpr evaluation hit maximum step limit'; raise -fconstexpr-ops-limit (GCC) or -fconstexpr-steps (Clang).
Without <experimental/simd>, find only accepts sets of 64 entries or fewer (requires-clause). Sets above 64 entries use SIMD buckets sized to the native register width.

Main has an untagged change made after the v5.0.5 tag (PR #18, July 2025), still in the v5_0_5 inline namespace. The change narrows the probe key to the 32/64-bit mask type before find compares it with the full stored key. From reading the code (not compiled), keys longer than 4 bytes whose mask fits in 32 bits may stop matching, and no self-test covers this case. Pin tag v5.0.5 or test your key set.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick mph over frozen or gperf when your keys are integers, enums or strings of 8 bytes or fewer on x86-64 with BMI2 and per-lookup latency matters most. The author's plots put it below frozen, gperf and boost::unordered_flat_map up to 1024 keys, and there is no head-to-head with Kronuz constexpr-phf or ConstexprCore/perfect_hash. Pick frozen instead for C++14, MSVC, longer strings or a container API; pick gperf or triehash for long string keys or generated C code.
verified_claims_summary: In the author's nanobench run, lookups were random hits drawn from sets of 5-100 strings of 1-8 bytes. It used clang++ and g++ with -O3 -mbmi2 and libstdc++ on the g++ run; no CPU model or compiler versions are given. mph measured 1.4-7.2 ns per lookup, against 5.3-25.4 ns for std::unordered_map (with boost::hash) and 7.7-13.1 ns for gperf. The lead over gperf shrinks to 1.3-2.2x on the variable-length sets. The harness calls the v2-era mph::hash/mph::fixed_string API, which the current header no longer has, so the tables predate the current lookup/find code.
